words.meaning: Reverse a situation so that the person or group previously at a disadvantage gains the advantage.
words.pattern: turn the tables on someone · turn the tables with a stronger offer
words.cue: the weaker side gains the upper hand
words.example: A reliable replenishment service helped the smaller brand turn the tables on its larger rival.
words.everydayExample: After losing the first game, I turned the tables on my brother in the rematch.
words.usageNote: Keep tables plural and use on before the opponent. This means reversing an advantage, not simply changing a situation; turn a corner means begin to improve.
words.recallPrompt: Describe how a weaker competitor could turn the tables on a market leader.

words.meaning: A flat disc, typically made of vinyl, with grooves that reproduce recorded sound when played on a record player.
words.pattern: play / collect a vinyl record · a vinyl collection · a record player
words.cue: a grooved music disc, not a CD
words.example: The brand partnered with a record shop to produce a limited-edition vinyl record for a launch event.
words.everydayExample: I found an old vinyl record in a second-hand shop.
words.usageNote: Stress the first syllable of the noun record: RE-cord, unlike the verb re-CORD. Vinyl is often uncountable for the medium: I collect vinyl. Vinyl records is the clearest plural for individual discs.
words.recallPrompt: Describe a vinyl record to someone who has only streamed music.

words.register: Informal; admiring or critical depending on context
words.meaning: A person who enjoys taking dangerous risks; as an adjective, describing daring, risky acts or the people who perform them.
words.pattern: a daredevil · a daredevil stunt / rider · something of a daredevil
words.example: The safety director rejected a daredevil stunt proposed for the brand's promotional event.
words.everydayExample: My cousin is a daredevil who loves extreme sports.
words.usageNote: Not a neutral synonym for brave: it can suggest recklessness. Use courageous or highly trained for professionals managing necessary risks. The adjective is normally used before a noun.
words.recallPrompt: Explain the difference between a courageous decision and daredevil behaviour.

words.meaning: Pause until you can breathe comfortably again after exertion; figuratively, take a short rest after intense activity. It can also describe a sudden intake of breath from surprise or emotion.
words.pattern: stop / pause to catch my breath · give someone a moment to catch their breath
words.example: After the intense launch period, the team needed a day to catch its breath before starting the next phase.
words.everydayExample: I stopped halfway up the hill to catch my breath.
words.usageNote: Change the possessive to match the subject. Breath /breθ/ is a noun; breathe /briːð/ is a verb. Past: caught my breath. Catch my breath usually means recover; hold my breath means deliberately stop breathing for a time.
words.recallPrompt: Describe a busy period after which you needed to catch your breath.

words.register: Neutral; common in business and conversation
words.meaning: Surprise someone when they are unprepared, often leaving them unsure how to respond.
words.pattern: catch someone off guard · be caught off guard by a question / announcement
words.example: The retailer's sudden order cancellation caught the planning team off guard.
words.everydayExample: Her unexpected compliment caught me off guard.
words.usageNote: Caught is the past tense and past participle of catch. It can describe pleasant as well as unpleasant surprises. Write off guard without a hyphen in this pattern; not caught of guard.
words.recallPrompt: Describe a question that caught you off guard and how you responded.

words.register: Informal; often British, humorous, or old-fashioned
words.meaning: An exaggerated way of saying that someone may become very ill with a cold, often used to urge them to wear warmer or drier clothes.
words.pattern: You'll catch your death! · catch your death of cold
words.cue: put a coat on, says the exaggerated warning
words.example: As colleagues left the site in the rain, one joked, You'll catch your death without a coat! The formal safety notice used plain instructions instead.
words.everydayExample: Put something warm on—you'll catch your death out there!
words.usageNote: Not usually a literal prediction of death and not appropriate for serious safety or medical advice. Colds are caused by viruses; the idiom must not be taught as proof that cold weather itself causes infection. Change your to my, his, or her as needed.
words.recallPrompt: Use the expression in a clearly informal, exaggerated warning about going out without a coat.

words.meaning: A simple solution expected to solve a difficult problem quickly and completely, often used to say that no such solution exists.
words.pattern: a magic bullet for a problem · there is no magic bullet · look for a magic bullet
words.cue: one easy fix for a complex problem
words.example: AI is not a magic bullet for poor planning; processes, data, and accountability still matter.
words.everydayExample: There is no magic bullet for keeping a busy household organised.
words.usageNote: Usually countable: a magic bullet, not magic bullet alone. Silver bullet is a similar metaphor. The expression can signal scepticism about oversimplified promises; it does not establish a product's effectiveness.
words.recallPrompt: Explain why one technology is not a magic bullet for a business problem.

words.meaning: A substance that a living organism needs for growth, maintenance, or normal functioning.
words.pattern: an essential nutrient · provide / absorb nutrients · nutrient content
words.cue: a substance the body or plant needs
words.example: The product team compared the nutrient content of the two formulations before discussing any claims.
words.everydayExample: The gardener added compost to replenish nutrients in the soil.
words.usageNote: Nutrient is a countable substance; nutrition refers to nourishment or the field of study. Nutritious means providing useful nourishment; nutritional means related to nutrition. A nutrient is not necessarily a vitamin.
words.recallPrompt: Use nutrient and nutrition in two sentences that show the difference.

words.meaning: Containing a relatively small amount of saturated fat, a category of dietary fat. The phrase describes that feature only, not the food's entire nutritional quality.
words.pattern: a food / diet low in saturated fat · be low in saturated fat · high in fibre
words.cue: a small amount of one type of fat
words.example: The team checked the composition data before describing the prototype as low in saturated fat.
words.everydayExample: I compared the labels to see which option was low in saturated fat.
words.usageNote: Use low in + substance, not low of. Low in saturated fat is not the same as low in total fat, fat-free, or automatically healthy overall. This entry teaches the phrase, not a numerical labelling threshold or personal dietary recommendation; verify evidence before making a product claim.
words.recallPrompt: Describe one product feature using low in, then explain what that description does not tell you.

questions.prompt: Complete the idiom: The underdog managed to turn the ________ on its rival.
questions.note: Turn the tables on someone means reverse the balance of advantage.

questions.prompt: Use today's two-word noun phrase for a grooved music disc: a ________.
questions.note: Record is a noun here, with stress on its first syllable.

questions.prompt: Use today's noun: A person who enjoys dangerous risks is a ________.
questions.note: Daredevil can imply recklessness; it is not always straightforward praise.

questions.prompt: Complete the noun: I stopped running to catch my ________.
questions.note: Breath is the noun; breathe is the verb.

questions.prompt: Complete the pattern: The unexpected question caught me ________ guard.
questions.note: Caught someone off guard means surprised them when unprepared.

questions.prompt: Complete the exaggerated informal warning: Put your coat on or you'll catch your ________!
questions.note: Catch your death is hyperbole, not a literal prediction or medical explanation.

questions.prompt: Use today's two-word metaphor: There is no ________ for a complex planning problem.
questions.note: A magic bullet is an imagined simple, complete solution.

questions.prompt: Use today's noun in the plural: Plants absorb essential ________ from their environment.
questions.note: Nutrients are substances; nutrition is nourishment or its study.

questions.prompt: Complete the preposition: This option is low ________ saturated fat.
questions.note: Use low in or high in a nutrient or ingredient.

story.title: The launch that needed more than a slogan
paragraphs: Maya's FMCG team planned a small product launch with a local record shop. A DJ would play a vinyl record while guests tried the prototype. An overnight forecast of heavy rain caught her off guard, and she took a moment to catch her breath before moving the event indoors.

The agency suggested rescuing the publicity with a daredevil outdoor stunt. Maya refused. As a colleague ran in without a coat, the DJ joked, You'll catch your death out there! Everyone laughed, but the team kept its actual safety instructions clear and practical.

Inside, a marketer wanted one dramatic health slogan. Maya reminded him that there was no magic bullet for earning trust. The nutrient data mattered: even if a product was low in saturated fat, that alone did not describe its overall nutritional quality.
The team used clear information, a good tasting experience, and reliable availability instead of hype. Those strengths gave the small brand a chance to turn the tables on its larger rival.
